abstract: Narayanan and Kapoor argue AI is best understood as a 'normal' general-purpose technology — diffusion-bottlenecked by organizations, regulation, complementary capital, and human adoption — rather than a discontinuous economic singularity. They predict gradual, sectorally uneven labor impacts and warn against policy frames built on transformative-AGI assumptions.
keyFindings: AI deployment is rate-limited by complementary investments (data, integration, training, regulation), not by model capability
Predicts gradual labor reallocation rather than mass displacement; sectoral patterns will resemble prior GPT cycles
Warns that policy and investment built around AGI-soon assumptions misallocates resources
Argues most observable AI productivity gains come from narrow, well-scoped task automation rather than open-ended autonomous agents
methodology: Essay synthesizing diffusion economics, technology history, and current empirical AI deployment patterns.
qualifiers: Tier 3 essay. Authors are computer scientists, not labor economists; conclusions depend on the GPT analogy holding. Counters more aggressive timelines (Aschenbrenner, Amodei) but is not itself an empirical study.
